title_original: Beyond Silence: Tegene Kunbi Challenges the Boundaries of African Abstraction at Venice
excerpt_original: At Ethiopia’s second national pavilion at the Venice Biennale, artist Tegene Kunbi and assistant curator Yohannes Mulat Mekonnen challenge the expectation that African painting must explain itself through identity, politics or cultural inheritance in Shapes […]

blocks.text: At Ethiopia’s second national pavilion at the Venice Biennale, artist Tegene Kunbi and assistant curator Yohannes Mulat Mekonnen challenge the expectation that African painting must explain itself through identity, politics or cultural inheritance in Shapes of Silence . In conversation with Suzette Bell-Roberts, they explore the relationship between colour and silence, the influence of Ethiopian artistic traditions, and abstraction’s freedom to resist imposed meanings.

Vast fields of saturated colour collide with patterned textiles, glittering surfaces and geometric forms in Tegene Kunbi’s monumental paintings. Some stretch four metres across, their layered compositions shifting between architectural order and intricate material detail. Fabrics interrupt painted surfaces, carrying traces of domestic life, religious traditions and journeys across Africa. Yet these visually exuberant works belong to Shapes of Silence , Ethiopia’s second national pavilion at the Venice Biennale, curated by Abebaw Ayalew at Palazzo Bollani. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: Kunbi transforms textiles gathered across the continent into complex abstract compositions where personal memory encounters collective history. Fabrics recalling his mother, Mulu Lema, and her textile practice coexist with materials drawn from different cultural traditions, their distinct identities preserved within the paintings. Rather than illustrating specific narratives, his work explores how colour, texture and material relationships can hold difference without resolving it.

Kunbi and assistant curator Yohannes Mulat Mekonnen challenge established narratives of abstraction, exploring its roots in Ethiopian artistic traditions, personal memory and cultural exchange while questioning why African painting is so often expected to justify its meaning through identity and politics. Kunbi also reflects on his exchanges with Koyo Kouoh, whose In Minor Keys shares the exhibition’s understanding of silence as an essential element of expression. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: Your paintings are monumental, intensely colourful and materially complex, yet the exhibition is titled Shapes of Silence . Where does silence exist within such an expressive visual language?

Tegene Kunbi: “The colourful is also the silence.” For me, silence is not necessarily the absence of colour or expression. It exists within the process of painting, through the accumulation of materials, the relationships between colours and the moment when a composition reaches completion. I experience silence through making rather than trying to illustrate it.

Yohannes Mulat Mekonnen: Silence is not absence. It can be understood as an equilibrium between contrasting elements. Tegene brings together strong colours and materials carrying different histories, allowing them to coexist within a single composition. Their differences remain visible, but relationships emerge between them. In music, a continuous note cannot establish rhythm without interruption. The pauses are as important as the sounds themselves. Silence therefore becomes one condition through which expression acquires structure. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: You have described encountering abstraction in your home rather than in a museum. How have Ethiopian cultural traditions and everyday experiences shaped your understanding of abstraction independently of Western art history?

TK: “I didn’t see abstraction in a museum. I see my home.” Abstraction was already present in my surroundings, in music, poetry, architecture and everyday experiences. I didn’t discover it through European art history. These ways of thinking and seeing were part of the cultural environment I grew up in. “Our life is also abstract.” Abstraction shapes how we experience the world, remember, and understand things beyond their immediate appearance.

YMM: Ethiopian painting traditions, particularly Orthodox Christian iconography, offer important perspectives on abstraction. In these traditions, representation does not necessarily follow European conventions of naturalism or perspective. Figures and objects may be organised by spiritual significance rather than by their position in physical space. The intention is not always to reproduce material reality, but to communicate spiritual phenomena beyond naturalistic description. These histories challenge the assumption that abstraction originated exclusively within European modernism before being adopted elsewhere. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: Textiles collected across Africa appear alongside materials that recall your mother, Mulu Lema, and your childhood. How do these personal memories change when incorporated into paintings that also carry wider cultural histories?

TK: Textiles have deep personal significance for me, especially through my memories of my mother and her work with fabrics. In our home, we used textiles to cover valued household objects. They were part of everyday life, but they also represented care and cultural continuity. “For me, it brings me, my mother.” Through my travels across Africa, I have encountered many different materials and traditions. When I bring these textiles into my paintings, they retain those personal associations while forming new relationships with colour and form.

YMM: These materials operate within both personal and collective histories. Some are associated with domestic life, others with religious ceremonies, clothing and different cultural practices. They carry distinct histories, but within the paintings they establish relationships without losing their individual characteristics. The viewer does not necessarily need to recognise the origins of every material. What becomes important is how these histories encounter one another through the painting. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: You have suggested that excessive interpretation can effectively silence a painting. Where should curatorial explanation end and the viewer’s freedom to encounter a work on its own terms begin?

YMM: “This hierarchical relation makes painting silent.” Titles, curatorial statements and theoretical interpretations can establish a hierarchy in which language determines how a painting should be understood. This becomes problematic when explanation takes precedence over the artwork itself. Interpretation is important, but there is a difference between providing context and prescribing meaning. A painting has its own visual and material language. Curatorial interpretation should open possibilities for understanding rather than restrict the viewer to a predetermined reading. Tegene Kunbi, Woven Earth , 2026, Oil and textile on canvas, 300 × 299 × 4 cm. Courtesy of the artist

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi, Woven Earth , 2026, Oil and textile on canvas, 300 × 299 × 4 cm. Courtesy of the artist

blocks.text: Ethiopian Orthodox painting traditions offer approaches to representation that differ fundamentally from European naturalism. How might recognising these histories change the way African abstraction is positioned within international art history?

YMM: Ethiopian Orthodox painting demonstrates that visual traditions have long existed outside European conventions of perspective and representation. In these works, spiritual significance can determine composition, scale and spatial relationships. The objective is not necessarily to reproduce visible reality, but to communicate experiences and phenomena beyond naturalistic description.

Recognising these histories allows us to reconsider the assumption that abstraction emerged primarily through European modernism. Tegene’s development from earlier engagement with religious imagery towards an increasingly abstract language can be understood within a longer Ethiopian artistic trajectory. It is not simply a movement from tradition towards modernity. Different cultures have developed their own intellectual and visual frameworks for abstraction, many of which remain marginalised within international art history. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: The paintings bring together materials associated with different communities, histories and cultural practices. Against Ethiopia’s contemporary political divisions, what possibilities does abstraction offer for expressing coexistence without suggesting that differences have been resolved?

TK: Travelling through Mauritania, Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya and Madagascar has allowed me to encounter different materials, music and symbolic forms. These experiences have made me curious about where cultural expressions originate and how they travel between communities. When I bring different materials together in a painting, they establish relationships through colour, texture and composition. Their differences remain part of the work.

YMM: Ethiopia’s ethnic, linguistic and religious diversity has become deeply entangled with contemporary political tensions. The incorporation of textiles associated with different regions and communities can be understood as a symbolic gesture towards unity. Materials whose differences have acquired political significance become part of a shared composition.

This does not mean that abstraction resolves political divisions. Rather, the paintings allow different histories and identities to coexist without requiring uniformity. They suggest that cultural relationships extend beyond the divisions through which communities are sometimes defined. Tegene Kunbi. Dale Grant Photography, © Dale Grant. Courtesy of the artist

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Dale Grant Photography, © Dale Grant. Courtesy of the artist

blocks.text: Your conversations with Koyo Kouoh explored abstraction and African artistic identity. What did those exchanges challenge or affirm in your thinking, particularly in relation to the expectations placed upon African artists internationally?

TK: I knew Koyo personally, and we exchanged ideas about abstraction and African artistic identity. Those conversations shaped my thinking about painting beyond established interpretative frameworks. African artists are often expected to explain their work through cultural identity, politics or history. These histories are important, but they should not become the only way our work is understood. Abstraction offers possibilities that cannot always be reduced to explanation. Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.caption: Tegene Kunbi. Shapes of Silence. Padiglione Etiopia alla 61. Esposizione Internazionale d’Arte – La Biennale di Venezia. Foto: Alice Zorzin / Volcano Visual Studio

blocks.text: At the Venice Biennale, national pavilions inevitably frame artists through questions of cultural identity and representation. What would it mean for African painting to be encountered without the expectation that it must explain its origins, politics or cultural significance?

YMM: Cultural and historical contexts are important, but they should not determine every interpretation of an artwork. African artists are often expected to account for their work through identity, politics, and cultural inheritance, even when similar expectations are not placed on European abstraction.

Within a national pavilion, these questions become particularly significant because artistic practice is inevitably associated with national representation. Yet Tegene’s paintings draw upon Ethiopian traditions while incorporating materials and experiences from across Africa. They demonstrate that cultural belonging is not necessarily confined to national boundaries.
The challenge is to recognise the histories informing a painting without making those histories its only possible meaning. Context should deepen our engagement with art, not restrict its freedom.
